summary: Describes a class of BGP configurations with more than one stable outcome, where the state actually reached may be unintended and equally stable. Such configurations are called BGP Wedgies. It challenges the common belief that BGP always produces forwarding paths in a deterministic way. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a ball that can settle in two different dips. Sometimes the internet routes settle in the wrong dip and stay stuck there, even though the right one is also stable.

subtitle: When routing policies trap the internet in stable but unintended states.

tldr.problem: BGP is generally assumed to create forwarding paths in a deterministic manner. However, certain configurations of routing policies can create situations where multiple stable forwarding states exist, some of which are unintended.
tldr.mechanism: When autonomous systems use local preference settings to prefer customer routes over peer routes, and employ primary/backup policies with path prepending, complex interactions can occur. BGP may converge to a stable state that does not match the network administrator's intent, and remain stuck there.
tldr.outcome: These unintended stable states, called BGP Wedgies, reveal a fundamental limitation: BGP can reach multiple stable outcomes from a single configuration, and may select these outcomes non-deterministically. Recovering from a wedgied state may require deliberately disrupting service.

today: RFC 4264 remains informational analysis of a fundamental issue in BGP routing. It has not been obsoleted or updated. BGP wedgies continue to be a real operational challenge for network administrators managing complex peering relationships and traffic engineering policies.

sections.title: BGP and Determinism
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the routing protocol that ties the internet together, distributing reachability information between autonomous systems. A fundamental assumption has been that BGP creates forwarding paths in a deterministic manner: given a configuration, BGP should reliably produce a single intended routing outcome.

This memo challenges that assumption. Certain classes of BGP configurations can have multiple stable forwarding states, and BGP may converge to an unintended state that is equally stable as the intended state. Network administrators may have no way to predict or recover from this situation without disrupting service or possessing knowledge of remote network configurations.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP is the system that routes traffic between the big internet providers. We thought it always worked the same way, but it turns out it can get stuck in wrong ways.

sections.title: Routing Policies and Preferences
sections.content:
Network administrators use BGP policies to optimize their network's cost, performance, and reliability. Cost optimization commonly involves preferring customer-originated routes (which bring revenue) over routes from peers or upstream transit providers. Administrators also employ primary and backup upstream providers for redundancy, preferring the primary link for normal operation and the backup only during failures.

These preferences are expressed through local preference attributes and AS path prepending, where the local AS number is repeated to artificially lengthen the path to make certain routes less preferred. Alternatively, BGP communities allow upstream providers to publish values that customers can use to mark routes as backup-only or primary-preferred, with local preference overriding path length. These mechanisms are individually reasonable, but their interactions can create unexpected outcomes.
sections.plainLanguage: Network operators set up rules like 'use this provider first, that one as backup.' These rules locally make sense, but when all the networks apply their rules together, strange things can happen.

sections.title: Simple BGP Wedgies
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates a simple wedgie with four autonomous systems: AS1 advertises routes marked as primary to AS4 and backup to AS2. AS4 advertises those routes to AS3, and AS3 advertises them to AS2. Normally, AS2 prefers the longer path through AS3 and AS4 because the direct path is marked backup-only. This is the intended state.

However, if the AS1-AS4 link breaks and then is restored, a problem arises. AS3 learns the primary path from AS4, but AS3's policy prefers customer-advertised routes (from AS2) over peer routes (from AS4). So AS3 continues to prefer the path through AS2 even after the primary path is restored. The network is now wedged: traffic to AS1 continues over the backup path despite the primary being available. Restoring the intended state requires AS1 to deliberately disconnect from AS2, disrupting traffic, just to reset the BGP state.
sections.plainLanguage: In the simplest case, a network gets stuck using the backup route even after the main route comes back. The only way to fix it is to break the backup link on purpose.

sections.title: Multi-Party Wedgies
sections.content:
The situation becomes more complex with three or more upstream providers. If AS1 has three upstream providers with one primary and two backup, and the link between two of the backup providers breaks and is restored, the network can become wedged in a way where resetting a single link does not help. Instead, traffic switches between the two backup providers without returning to the primary.

Fixing this requires AS1 to simultaneously reset links to both backup providers, which is not intuitive: at any given moment, only one backup link carries traffic, yet both must be brought down together. This demonstrates that the knowledge required to understand and fix a wedgie is not localized; the network administrator must understand the topology and policies of distant networks to determine the correct sequence of actions.
sections.plainLanguage: With more providers involved, the problem gets worse. You might have to break multiple connections at the same time, which is hard to figure out.

sections.title: Non-Determinism and Stability
sections.content:
BGP exhibits both intended and unintended non-determinism. Intended non-determinism includes cases like tie-breaking between equally-preferred routes by preferring the longest-lived route. Unintended non-determinism arises from unexpected policy interactions: multiple stable BGP states exist, and which state the protocol converges to is not predictable from local configuration alone.

The paradox is that as network topology becomes denser and routing policies become more expressive (to engineer traffic more precisely), the number of unintended stable states increases. BGP wedgies reveal that there is insufficient local information for a single network administrator to identify root causes or determine the correct recovery sequence. As complexity increases, deterministic traffic engineering through BGP becomes increasingly difficult to guarantee.
sections.plainLanguage: The fundamental issue is that each network runs its own local rules, but the rules interact in ways nobody completely predicted. More rules and more connections make it harder, not easier, to predict what will happen.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
BGP wedgies create a potential attack surface. A hostile third party can deliberately cause a BGP session to reset, triggering the conditions that lead to an unintended forwarding state. The impact of this state—increased cost, reduced bandwidth, higher latency, or degraded reliability—may be long-lived, far outlasting the temporary connectivity interruption that triggered it.

An attacker need not modify routing information; merely disrupting a peering session can flip the network into an unintended state. This is particularly concerning because the knowledge required to fix the problem may not be available to affected network administrators, and the recovery may require coordinated multi-party actions or service disruptions. The RFC notes that BGP contains no specific mechanisms to prevent unauthorized modification of routing information, and this memo introduces no new security mechanisms—it simply illustrates a class of behavior that may be exploitable.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can break one link and flip your network into a bad state. It might take a long time to recover from that, and you may not even know why it happened.
